summary:
Same-sex relations are not criminalised in Cabo Verde. The employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation but does not extend to gender identity, leaving trans workers without an explicit statutory basis for workplace complaints (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. As of 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory contains no later statute or administrative route for legal gender change.

Same-sex unions are not recognised. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Public visibility is high: LGBTIQ organisations register freely, the country held its first public Pride in 2013 (the second in Africa), and Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group, making anti-discrimination commitments in its 2024 Universal Periodic Review. Polling from 2019 to 2021 found 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour.

Trans-specific violence has been reported. Tchinda Andrade described verbal violence and two physical attacks, while characterising Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed (Rede Angola, 22 June 2016).
tangentialFactors:
Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020) groups Cabo Verde with Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe as particularly tolerant African countries, while noting that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains weak even among younger respondents across the continent.

The 2018 Pride Week in Praia included a parade and NGO campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia and Associação Arco Iris, which petitioned the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women were engaged (Equal Eyes, 20 July 2018).
localsOnly:
Residents have access to freely registering LGBTIQ organisations and an established annual Pride presence since 2013. Workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is prohibited, but gender identity is not a protected ground.

Legal name and gender change remains unavailable under civil law as of the latest sourced account (2016). No later statute or administrative procedure is recorded in the source inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any legal gender recognition procedure has been adopted after 2016 is unresolved; the source inventory contains no statute or administrative route dated later than the 2016 account.

The scope of the employment discrimination protection (which statute establishes it, and whether it covers housing, education, or healthcare as well as employment) is not sourced here.

No sourced information was found on gender-marker rules for passports or other travel documents, airport or border screening practices, access to trans-specific healthcare, or hate-crime sentencing enhancements.
